cluster_name: US unveils 'Operation Economic Outcast' secondary sanctions targeting Iran trading partners
tldr: At the headline layer, militarised economic language — 'D-Day,' 'asphyxiation,' 'onslaught,' 'endgame' — dominates across all 34 outlets in 21 countries with near-total uniformity, a narrower and more aggressive register than body text typically sustains. The third-country coercion angle (secondary sanctions, dollar-system exclusion threats) is a secondary but prominent headline theme across roughly a third of outlets, foregrounding the global ultimatum over the Iran-specific pressure. Iran's counter-threats — Gulf oil shutoff, vows to 'go on the attack' — surface in only five outlet headlines, meaning most reader-facing homepages advertised a one-directional US offensive rather than a two-sided escalation. Policy-effectiveness skepticism ('Will Work This Time,' 'We've heard that before,' 'opts for surprising moderation instead') is a visible minority current across four outlets from three different country groups, all from outlets with centrist or centre-left leans. Singapore's Straits Times stands as the sole outlet to directly contradict the D-Day build-up in its headline, reporting the US chose 'surprising moderation' — the sharpest headline-layer divergence from the US-administration framing in the entire corpus.
event_summary: On August 24, 2026, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced 'Operation Economic Outcast,' expanding US secondary sanctions to cover Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping, and threatening dollar-system exclusion for any country continuing to trade with Tehran.

single_outlet_findings.finding: The only headline in the corpus to directly contradict the US administration's D-Day framing: 'the US opts for surprising moderation instead' inverts the crisis register that 33 other outlets adopted verbatim or amplified — a uniquely Asia-Pacific editorial judgment that the announcement was a climb-down, not an offensive.

The only headline to frame the secondary sanctions as a binary ultimatum to the global financial order: 'Join new Iran sanctions or leave the dollar system' reframes the story from US-Iran bilateral pressure to a US-world coercion, a framing absent from all other 33 outlet headlines.

The only headline to invoke historical precedent as a punchline: 'We've heard that before' positions the D-Day rhetoric within a pattern of failed US endgame claims — a headline-layer form of policy skepticism that body text can sustain across paragraphs but which here appears in six words.

The only headline to frame the story through a 47-year timeline rather than today's announcement: 'The US has been imposing sanctions on Iran since 1979' foregrounds historical continuity over the D-Day novelty claim, the sole outlet to counter-program the 'unprecedented' narrative at the headline layer.

'We Are Entering The Endgame' — a direct quote from Bessent adopted as the headline — is the most triumphalist headline framing in the corpus, unique to the US conservative outlet space and absent from all centrist and international outlets that ran the same story on the same day.

bottom_line: The headline layer of this story is a near-uniform 'economic D-Day' consensus — 34 outlets in 21 countries advertised militarised economic war language on their homepages, with the third-country ultimatum (secondary sanctions, dollar exclusion) as the only secondary headline dimension, and Straits Times's 'surprising moderation instead' as the sole outlier that ruptured the offensive framing.
